query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Directional solidification of a refractory high‐entropy alloy will create an aligned, low‐misorientation grain structure that improves high‐temperature strength and creep resistance while preserving its room‐temperature mechanical performance and keeping density low.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally cast refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., a NbMoCrTiAl‐ or AlCoCrFeNiTi–based alloy) with an isotropic, randomly oriented polycrystalline microstructure.
generation.intervention: Processing the alloy by directional solidification to achieve an oriented, dendritic grain structure with reduced high‐angle grain boundaries in the primary loading direction.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under uniaxial tensile or compressive loading at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (approximately 700–900 °C) as well as creep tests at high temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Aligned dendritic grains with preferential orientation and minimized deleterious grain boundary networks, which channel the load more effectively and reduce stress concentrations at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: Directional solidification induces a microstructural texture that limits grain-boundary sliding and reduces dislocation pile-up by orienting the strongest crystallographic directions along the loading axis. This microstructural control enhances high-temperature strength and creep resistance without altering the alloy’s chemical composition—and thus without increasing density—and maintains sufficient ductility at room temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a conventionally cast alloy, the directionally solidified alloy is predicted to exhibit roughly a 50% increase in high-temperature strength (or comparable improvement in creep resistance metrics) while retaining comparable yield strength and ductility at room temperature, with no significant change in density.
generation.baseline: The mechanical behavior (strength, ductility, and creep performance) of the isotropic, conventionally cast refractory high-entropy alloy.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected for alloys with similar compositions capable of forming a stable BCC or similar phase and when the processing parameters (e.g., withdrawal rate, thermal gradient) are optimized to produce a well-textured microstructure. Outside these conditions or for compositions prone to detrimental phase formation during directional solidification, the improvement may not occur.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the improvement and its sensitivity to variations in processing conditions and alloy composition remain uncertain and require experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same refractory high-entropy alloy composition—one processed via conventional casting and the other via directional solidification with controlled thermal gradients. Perform microstructural characterization (using EBSD) to confirm grain alignment. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature (700–900 °C) tensile and creep tests under identical loading conditions.
measurements: Room-temperature yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility
High-temperature yield strength and creep rate under constant load
EBSD data to quantify the degree of grain alignment and misorientation angles
Density measurements to confirm no significant change in alloy density
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the directionally solidified samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than ~25–30% increase) in high-temperature mechanical properties (strength or reduced creep rate) compared to the conventionally cast samples, or if adverse effects on room-temperature performance or density are observed, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
